title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
statement: You get a list of intervals [start, end] and a list of query numbers. An interval covers a query if start <= query <= end, and its size is end - start + 1. For each query, find the size of the smallest interval that covers it, or -1 if none does. Return the answers in the order the queries were given.

example.caption: Query 4 is covered by [2,5] (size 4) and [4,6] (size 3). The smallest is 3.

idea.sentence: Answer the queries from smallest to largest. Push every interval that has started into a min-heap keyed by size, and pop those that already ended: the top is the answer.

jargon.plain: A container where the smallest item is always on top. Push and pop each cost about log of its size.
One whose end is before the current query. Later queries are not smaller, so it can never help again.
Do not hunt for expired items. Only pop them when they reach the top and block the answer.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the intervals, then the queries, e.g. [[1,3],[2,3],[2,5],[4,6]], [4,2,6,3]

compare.bruteLabel: Scan every interval for every query

rows.name: Scan all intervals per query
rows.note: For each query, test every interval and keep the smallest that covers it.

rows.name: Sorted sweep with a min-heap
rows.note: Two sorts, then every interval is pushed once and popped at most once, each in log n.

fast.takeaway: Sorting the queries makes expiry permanent: once an interval ends before a query, it ends before every later one too.

stages.title: Sort both
stages.note: Sort a copy of the intervals by start. Sort the query positions by query value, so original positions survive.

stages.title: Push started intervals
stages.note: Push every interval that starts at or before the query, as (size, end), ordered by size.

stages.title: Pop expired
stages.note: While the smallest interval ends before the query, pop it. It is useless for all later queries too.

stages.title: Read the answer
stages.note: The top is the smallest interval still covering the query. Store its size at the query's original position, or -1.

stages.title: Return
stages.note: The answers array is already in the original query order.

edges.title: Queries out of order
edges.why: Queries are served smallest first, but each answer is written to its own original slot.

edges.title: Nothing covers it
edges.why: Query 4 falls in a gap and 1 and 7 are outside everything. An empty heap after popping means -1.

edges.title: Size counts both ends
edges.why: Size is end - start + 1, because both ends are included. A single point has size 1, not 0.

edges.title: No queries
edges.why: The loop never runs. Return an empty list, not null.

gotchas.text: Do not sort the queries array itself and return it. You would lose which answer belongs to which query. Sort a list of positions instead, and write answer[pos].
Pop expired intervals only from the top. An expired interval buried under a smaller live one is harmless, and it is popped later when it surfaces.
Sorting numbers needs a comparator: (a, b) => queries[a] - queries[b]. Without it the default sort compares as strings and puts 10 before 9, which breaks the expiry logic.
intervals.sort(...) reorders the caller's array. Sort a copy with [...intervals]. There is no built-in heap, so a small class is included.

sort.Slice reorders the caller's slice, which shares memory, so copy it first. With container/heap, call heap.Push(h, x) and heap.Pop(h), not the methods on h directly. Make the answer with make([]int, len(queries)) so it is [] and not nil for no queries.

recap.pattern: Intervals: sweep queries with a min-heap
recap.key: Process queries smallest first. Push intervals as they start, pop those that ended, and the top (smallest size) answers the query.
recap.complexity: Time O((n + m) log(n + m)). Space O(n + m).
moves: Sort intervals by start; sort query positions by value
Push each interval with start <= query as (size, end)
Pop while the top ends before the query
Answer is the top size, or -1; store at the original position
